title: Extract a list of all employee names from the employee list.
shortTitle: Extract a list of all employee names from the employee list
keyPoints: map() applies a Function<T,R> to each element, producing a new stream of the transformed values
Employee::getName is a method reference equivalent to the lambda e -> e.getName()
map is strictly one-to-one: every input produces exactly one output, so the output stream has the same size

s1_definition.oneliner: `map` transforms each element into something else, one in and one out, producing a new stream of the results.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **`Stream.map(Function<T,R>)`** applies a one-argument function to every element, producing a new stream of transformed values.
- **Method reference** `Employee::getName` is preferred over the lambda `e -> e.getName()` when simply calling an existing getter.
- **One-to-one** relationship: every input element produces exactly one output element.
- **Terminal collector** `collect(Collectors.toList())` or Java 16+ `toList()` materialises the stream.
- The source collection is **never modified**; map produces a brand-new stream.
s1_definition.analogy: The HR clerk at the National Bank of India has a stack of full employee files but the manager only wants a printed list of names. She goes through each file and copies just the name onto a fresh sheet. `map` is that act of pulling one piece out of each item to build a new, simpler list.

sections.s2_detail:
### What does map() do?

The `map` method on a stream takes a `Function<T, R>` and applies it to every element, transforming type T into type R. For name extraction the function takes an `Employee` and returns its name `String`, so `map` changes the stream's element type from `Employee` to `String`. The relationship is strictly one-to-one: every input produces exactly one output, so the output stream has the same number of elements as the input.

### How do you extract employee names with map()?

You can write the function as a lambda `e -> e.getName()` or, more concisely, as a method reference `Employee::getName`. The method reference is preferred when it simply calls an existing method, because it is shorter and signals intent clearly.

```java
package com.bank.hr;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class ExtractNames {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Employee> staff = List.of(
            new Employee("Rajesh",  "Loans",   new BigDecimal("95000")),
            new Employee("Priya",   "IT",      new BigDecimal("120000")),
            new Employee("Amit",    "Finance", new BigDecimal("85000")),
            new Employee("Kavita",  "Loans",   new BigDecimal("78000")));

        // Using method reference
        List<String> names = staff.stream()
            .map(Employee::getName)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());

        System.out.println(names);
    }
}
```

```text
[Rajesh, Priya, Amit, Kavita]
```

### How is map() different from flatMap()?

| Feature | map() | flatMap() |
|---|---|---|
| Relationship | One-to-one | One-to-many |
| Return type of function | Single value R | Stream<R> |
| Flattening | No | Yes, merges inner streams |
| Use case | Extract a field | Expand nested collections |

```java
// map: one Employee -> one String (name)
staff.stream().map(Employee::getName);

// flatMap: one Department -> many Employees
departments.stream().flatMap(d -> d.getEmployees().stream());
```

### What are common mistakes?

Mistake: trying to use map when the function returns a collection, then wondering why the result is a list of lists.

```java
// WRONG: map returns Stream<List<String>>, not Stream<String>
List<List<String>> nested = departments.stream()
    .map(Department::getEmployeeNames)   // each dept returns a List<String>
    .collect(Collectors.toList());       // List<List<String>>

// CORRECT: use flatMap to flatten
List<String> flat = departments.stream()
    .flatMap(d -> d.getEmployeeNames().stream())
    .collect(Collectors.toList());       // List<String>
```

### What about Java 16+ toList()?

Java 16 introduced `Stream.toList()` as a convenience terminal operation that returns an unmodifiable list.

```java
// Java 8-15
List<String> names = staff.stream()
    .map(Employee::getName)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());   // mutable ArrayList

// Java 16+
List<String> names = staff.stream()
    .map(Employee::getName)
    .toList();                       // unmodifiable list
```

The key difference is that `toList()` returns an unmodifiable list, so calling `names.add("New")` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. Use `collect(Collectors.toList())` when you need to mutate the result.

### What about null safety?

If any employee's name could be null, the map itself does not fail, but downstream operations such as sorting or joining might throw a NullPointerException.

```java
// Guard: filter nulls before downstream operations
List<String> safeNames = staff.stream()
    .map(Employee::getName)
    .filter(java.util.Objects::nonNull)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
```

### What about chaining map with other operations?

map is an intermediate operation, so it can be chained freely with filter, sorted, and other operations in a single pipeline.

```java
// Extract names of Loans department employees, sorted
List<String> loanNames = staff.stream()
    .filter(e -> "Loans".equals(e.getDepartment()))
    .map(Employee::getName)
    .sorted()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

System.out.println(loanNames);
```

```text
[Kavita, Rajesh]
```

### What should a senior engineer know?

- `map` is lazy: it does not execute until a terminal operation triggers the pipeline.
- `map` preserves encounter order on ordered streams, so the output list has the same order as the input.
- For primitive results use `mapToInt`, `mapToLong`, or `mapToDouble` to avoid boxing overhead.
- The source collection is never modified; `map` produces a brand-new stream, making it safe for concurrent reads.

### What are common interview follow-up questions?

- "What is the difference between map and flatMap?" map is one-to-one; flatMap is one-to-many with flattening.
- "Does map modify the source list?" No, it produces a new stream.
- "When would you use mapToInt instead of map?" When the result is a primitive int, to avoid boxing overhead.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To extract one field out of each object I use the map operation, which applies a function to every element and produces a new stream of the transformed values. For names I map with `Employee::getName`, which changes the stream's element type from Employee to String, and then I collect the result into a list. Because map is strictly one-to-one, the output list has exactly the same number of elements as the input.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this was a staff roll-call sheet for a branch meeting. The HR system stores rich employee objects with salary and department, but the meeting only needed a flat list of names, so I streamed the employees and mapped each one to just its name. I used a method reference rather than a full lambda because it simply calls an existing getter, which is shorter and signals the intent clearly.

The distinction between map and flatMap is a frequent interview discriminator. Map is one-to-one, so each input yields exactly one output and nothing is flattened. If my function had returned a collection for each element I would end up with a stream of collections, and that is exactly where flatMap is needed. On newer Java I can call `toList()` directly on the stream to get an unmodifiable list when I do not need to mutate the result.

Remember one sentence: `map(Employee::getName)` transforms each employee into its name string, one-to-one, and collect gathers them into a list.
